In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
[Ne II] is not a useful diagnostic of accretion in CTTSs.
[Ne II] is present in the inner regions of the disks around CTTSs, and that its line width is a sensitive probe of the physical conditions there.
[Ne II] is not a reliable indicator of the presence of a disk around CTTSs, but that it may be a good indicator of the presence or absence of a disk atmosphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
[Ne II] line emission in CTTS disks is weak, with a flux of 1-2% of that in the protoplanetary disk around the Herbig Ae star HD 163296.
the [Ne II]-based mass loss rate from the TW Hya disk is ~ 10-9 M ☉ yr-1, and that the mass loss rate is at most 10-11 M ☉ yr -1 for the other CTTSs.
the [Ne II]-emitting region in the disk around TW Hydrae has a size of ~ 0.1-0.3 AU and is optically thin, with a mass loss rate of ~ 10-10 M⊙ yr-1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the high-resolution [Ne II] observations are an important new tool for studying disk atmospheres and photoevaporation flows.
high-resolution spectroscopy can be a powerful tool for constraining the physical conditions and kinematics in protoplanetary disks.
[Ne II] is a potentially useful probe of disk atmospheres and outflows, but it is not a reliable tracer of disk rotation in CTTSs, as is the case for the [Fe II] 1.64 μm line.
